blocks.text: But we, having been invited, ate all the salted things, chennia, and cheeses, and salted goose fat. Hesychius: Χέννιον· ὀρνιθάριόν τι κατ᾽ Αἴγυπτον ταριχευόμενον [Chennion· ornitharion ti kat᾽ Aigypton taricheuomenon]; Chennium, a certain small bird in Egypt, preserved in salt. Since, then, there was so great an abundance of chennia and quails in Egypt and in all Africa, from where were they carried on the wings of the winds into the camp of the Israelites? There is no need here, as some do, to invent new miracles for ourselves, and to say that God created or multiplied the quails, as Christ multiplied the loaves in the hands of the Apostles. [col. 108] It is our part to hold fast to the sacred text, in which we do not read that the quails were created or multiplied by the power of God, but that they were brought by the winds from regions beyond the sea. I am not unaware that in the Vulgate version, Sap. XIX, 10., they are called a new creature of birds, and that many infer from this that God created them anew. But, to say nothing of the author of the book, to whom we have not bound our faith, the Greek copy does not have κτίσιν [ktisin], creature, but γένεσιν νέαν ὀρνέων [genesin nean orneōn], a new generation of birds; the Syriac likewise has ܡܘܠܕܐ ܚܕܬܐ ܕܦܪܚܬܐ, and the Arabic توالد طيور جديدة [tawālud ṭuyūr jadīda]. And it is called new not in itself, but to the Israelites, who had experienced nothing of the kind. Similar is the fact that the same author attributes to this very food ξένην γεῦσιν [xenēn geusin], a new taste, Sap. XVI, 2., that is, one unaccustomed and unknown to those who ate it. Here, therefore, we recognize no creation of quails. But this was miraculous: that they were brought in such great abundance, and at precisely the time that God had appointed, and that they all fell down around the camp of the Israelites, so as to serve them as food divinely provided.
